text: Cyanothamnus ramosus is a species of plant in the citrus family Rutaceae and is endemic to the southwest of Western Australia. It is an erect, mostly glabrous shrub that grows to a height of 30 cm (10 in), with pinnate leaves measuring 10–30 mm (0.4–1 in) long and having between three and seven leaflets on a petiole 1–11 mm (0.039–0.433 in) long; the leaflets are 5–15 mm (0.20–0.59 in) long. The plant produces up to three flowers in the leaf axils, on pedicels 2–15 mm (0.079–0.591 in) long, with four thick, glabrous, egg-shaped sepals 1.5–5 mm (0.059–0.20 in) long and white petals with blue or pale green backs, which are broadly elliptic, 3–5 mm (0.12–0.20 in) long and prominently glandular. Flowering occurs from May to October. The species was first formally described in 1839 by John Lindley, who named it Cyanothamnus ramosus in A Sketch of the Vegetation of the Swan River Colony. In 1863, George Bentham reclassified it as Boronia ramosa. In a 2013 paper in the journal Taxon, Marco Duretto and others restored Lindley's name Cyanothamnus ramosus based on cladistic analysis. The specific epithet "ramosus" is Latin for "full of branches." In 1971 and 1998, Paul Wilson described three subspecies in the journal Nuytsia, which have since been updated to reflect the genus change: subspecies anethifolius occurs between the Murchison River, the Stirling Range, and Cape Le Grand, subspecies lesueuranus is known only from near Mt Lesueur, and subspecies ramosus is mainly found in the Darling Range. The species is widespread on slopes and hillsides, sometimes in disused gravel pits, from near Shark Bay to near Esperance. Cyanothamnus ramosus is classified as "not threatened" by the Western Australian Government Department of Parks and Wildlife, but subspecies lesueuranus is listed as "Priority Two" by the Western Australian Government Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions, indicating it is poorly known and restricted to one or a few locations.
